chapter.title: How LLMs work
chapter.summary: From text to tokens to logits: the transformer forward pass, how models are pretrained and aligned, and how they are served fast and cheaply.

lessons.title: Tokens, embeddings and attention
lessons.summary: How text becomes token ids, ids become vectors, and a stack of transformer blocks with causal self-attention turns them into next-token logits.

parts.label: Concepts
parts.body:
## The one-sentence model

A large language model is a function that takes a sequence of token ids and returns, for every position, a probability distribution over the next token. Everything else (chat, tools, reasoning) is built by calling that function in a loop and appending what it picks.

```text
"The cat sat on the"  -> tokenizer -> [464, 3797, 3332, 319, 262]
                      -> transformer -> logits over ~100k-200k vocab at each position
                      -> softmax(last row) -> P(" mat") = 0.21, P(" floor") = 0.09, ...
                      -> sample " mat" -> append -> repeat
```

Three ideas carry the whole lesson: **tokens** (how text becomes integers), **embeddings** (how integers become vectors), and **attention** (how vectors at different positions exchange information).

## Tokenisation

Models never see characters or words. They see **token ids** from a fixed vocabulary. Modern LLMs use **subword** tokenisers, almost always a variant of **Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)**.

### How BPE is trained

1. Start with a base alphabet. Byte-level BPE (GPT-2 onwards) starts from the 256 possible bytes, so *any* UTF-8 string can be encoded and there is no "unknown token".
2. Pre-split the corpus (usually on whitespace and punctuation with a regex) so merges do not cross word boundaries.
3. Count every adjacent pair of symbols. Merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol and record the merge.
4. Repeat until the vocabulary reaches the target size.

```text
corpus words: low lower lowest
start:    l o w | l o w e r | l o w e s t
merge 1:  (l,o) -> lo      lo w | lo w e r | lo w e s t
merge 2:  (lo,w) -> low    low | low e r | low e s t
merge 3:  (e,r) -> er ...  low | low er | low e s t
```

Encoding new text replays the merges in the order they were learned. Common words become one token; rare words split into pieces; random strings fall back to bytes.

### Why it matters to an engineer

| Effect | Consequence |
|---|---|
| English averages roughly 4 characters (about 0.75 words) per token | Use it for back-of-envelope cost estimates, then measure with the real tokenizer |
| Many non-English scripts and code use more tokens per word | Same content costs more and uses more context in some languages |
| Numbers split unpredictably (`12345` may be `123` + `45`) | One reason models are shaky at digit-level arithmetic |
| Leading spaces are part of tokens (`" mat"` differs from `"mat"`) | Prompt formatting and trailing whitespace change what the model sees |
| Characters are hidden inside tokens | "How many r's in strawberry" style questions are hard without reasoning |
| Context limits, pricing and rate limits are all in tokens | Always count tokens with the provider's tokenizer, not `string.length` |

Vocabulary sizes have grown: GPT-2 used about 50k tokens, while recent model families use vocabularies in the 100k to 200k range. A bigger vocabulary means shorter sequences (cheaper attention, more text per context window) but a bigger embedding table and output layer.

**Special tokens** mark structure: beginning of sequence, end of turn, role headers in chat templates, tool-call delimiters. A "chat message" is really a string rendered through the model's **chat template** into a token sequence with these markers. Getting the template wrong is a classic fine-tuning bug.

## Embeddings

Each token id indexes a row of a learned matrix `E` with shape `[V, d_model]` (vocabulary size by model width). The lookup is just indexing, mathematically equivalent to multiplying a one-hot vector by `E`.

```text
ids  [T]            = [464, 3797, 3332]
E    [V, d_model]   = [100000, 4096]
X    [T, d_model]   = E[ids]          # 3 vectors of 4096 floats
```

These vectors start random and are trained with everything else. After training, directions in the space encode useful features (topic, syntax, sentiment), which is why similar tokens end up near each other. Note the difference from **embedding models** used in RAG: those output one vector per *passage*, produced by a whole network and trained with a contrastive objective. Input token embeddings are only the first layer of an LLM.

At the other end, an **unembedding** (LM head) matrix of shape `[d_model, V]` turns the final hidden vector back into one score (logit) per vocabulary token. Some models tie it to `E` (GPT-2 does), many recent large models keep it separate.

## The transformer block

The input vectors flow through a stack of `L` identical **blocks** (for example 32 in many 7B-8B models). Each block has two sub-layers, each wrapped in a residual connection:

```text
x = x + Attention(Norm(x))     # mix information ACROSS positions
x = x + MLP(Norm(x))           # transform each position INDEPENDENTLY
```

- **Self-attention** is the only place tokens talk to each other. Each position decides which earlier positions are relevant and pulls in a weighted mix of their information.
- The **MLP** (feed-forward network) is applied to each position separately. It holds most of the parameters and is where much factual association appears to be stored.
- The **residual stream** (`x = x + ...`) means every sub-layer *adds* to a running vector rather than replacing it. This keeps gradients healthy in deep stacks and lets layers specialise.
- **Normalisation** (LayerNorm or the cheaper RMSNorm) keeps activations in a stable range. Modern decoder models use **pre-norm**: normalise before the sub-layer, not after, which trains more stably than the original 2017 post-norm design.

## Position

Attention by itself is permutation-invariant: shuffle the tokens and each one computes the same weighted sums. Order must be injected.

| Scheme | Idea | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| Sinusoidal absolute | Add fixed sin/cos vectors to the input | Original Transformer |
| Learned absolute | Add a trained vector per position | GPT-2, BERT |
| **RoPE** | Rotate query and key vectors by a position-dependent angle | Llama, Mistral, Qwen and most open models today |
| ALiBi | Add a distance-based penalty to attention scores | Some models (e.g. BLOOM, MPT) |

RoPE is now the default. Because it rotates queries and keys, their dot product depends on the *relative* distance between positions, and context-extension tricks (changing the rotation base, interpolating positions) work by adjusting those angles.

## Decoder-only, causal

GPT-style LLMs are **decoder-only**: every position can attend only to itself and earlier positions (a **causal mask**). That one constraint makes training efficient: a single forward pass over a 4,096-token document yields 4,095 next-token predictions, each trained with cross-entropy against the true next token. Encoder models like BERT see both directions and are used for classification and embeddings, not for open-ended generation.

## Putting the pieces together

```text
token ids [T]
  -> embedding lookup              [T, d]
  -> L x (pre-norm attention + residual, pre-norm MLP + residual)
  -> final norm                    [T, d]
  -> LM head                       [T, V]   logits
  -> softmax over the last row     next-token distribution
```

The next tab works through the attention maths with exact shapes, then counts parameters and FLOPs for a real model.

parts.label: Under the hood
parts.body:
## Scaled dot-product attention

For one head, each position produces three vectors by linear projection of its (normalised) residual vector:

- **Query** `q`: what am I looking for?
- **Key** `k`: what do I contain, for matching?
- **Value** `v`: what do I hand over if selected?

```text
X   [T, d_model]
Q = X W_Q   [T, d_k]
K = X W_K   [T, d_k]
V = X W_V   [T, d_v]

scores  = Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)          [T, T]
scores += mask                       (-inf above the diagonal)
weights = softmax(scores, axis=-1)   [T, T]   each row sums to 1
out     = weights V                  [T, d_v]
```

Row `i` of `weights` says how much position `i` reads from every position `j <= i`. The output for position `i` is the weighted average of the value vectors.

**Why divide by `sqrt(d_k)`?** If `q` and `k` have independent components with unit variance, their dot product has variance `d_k`. With `d_k = 128`, raw scores would have a standard deviation around 11, pushing softmax into a near one-hot regime where gradients vanish. Scaling restores unit variance.

## The causal mask

```text
          keys ->  t0    t1    t2    t3
query t0        [  s    -inf  -inf  -inf ]
query t1        [  s     s    -inf  -inf ]
query t2        [  s     s     s    -inf ]
query t3        [  s     s     s     s   ]
```

Adding `-inf` before softmax gives those entries weight exactly zero, so position 2 can never peek at token 3. This is what lets training compute all next-token losses in parallel without cheating, and what makes the **KV cache** valid at inference: keys and values of past tokens never change when new tokens are appended.

## Multi-head attention

One attention pattern is limiting: a token may need its syntactic head, its antecedent and the previous token all at once. **Multi-head attention** runs `h` smaller attentions in parallel and concatenates them.

```text
d_model = 4096, h = 32  ->  d_head = 128

Q [T, 4096] -> reshape [T, 32, 128] -> transpose [32, T, 128]
scores per head   [32, T, T]
out per head      [32, T, 128] -> transpose/reshape [T, 4096]
final = out W_O   [T, 4096]      # mixes the heads back together
```

The cost is the same as a single big head (the projections are still `d_model x d_model`), but you get 32 independent attention patterns. Interpretability work has found heads that track previous tokens, copy repeated patterns (induction heads) and follow syntax.

### MQA and GQA

At inference the cached keys and values dominate memory. Two variants share them:

| Variant | Query heads | Key/value heads | KV cache vs MHA |
|---|---|---|---|
| Multi-head (MHA) | h | h | 1x |
| Grouped-query (GQA) | h | g (e.g. 8) | g/h (e.g. 1/4 with 32 query heads) |
| Multi-query (MQA) | h | 1 | 1/h |

Llama 3 8B, for example, uses 32 query heads and 8 key/value heads. GQA keeps most of MHA's quality with a fraction of the cache, which is why it became the default in open models.

## RoPE in one paragraph

Rotary position embedding treats each pair of dimensions `(x_{2i}, x_{2i+1})` of a query or key as a 2-D point and rotates it by angle `pos * theta_i`, where `theta_i = base^(-2i/d_head)` and `base` is typically 10,000 (larger in long-context models). Low-index pairs rotate quickly (fine position), high-index pairs slowly (coarse position). Because rotating `q` by angle `a` and `k` by angle `b` leaves their dot product depending only on `a - b`, attention scores depend on **relative** distance. RoPE is applied to Q and K only, never to V, and after the projection but before the dot product.

## The MLP

```text
classic (GPT-2):   MLP(x) = W_2 GELU(W_1 x)           W_1: [d, 4d], W_2: [4d, d]
SwiGLU (Llama):    MLP(x) = W_2 (SiLU(W_g x) * (W_1 x))  hidden size about (8/3) d
```

SwiGLU adds a gating projection, so the hidden width is shrunk to keep the parameter count similar. Llama 2 7B uses `d = 4096` and an MLP hidden size of 11,008.

## From the last hidden state to the next token

After the final block and final norm, each position has a vector `h_t` of size `d_model`. The LM head computes `logits_t = h_t W_U` with shape `[V]`. During training every row is used (cross-entropy against the true next token at each position). During generation only the **last** row matters:

```text
logits [T, V] -> take row T-1 -> divide by temperature -> softmax -> sample id
```

The training loss is the average negative log-probability the model gave to the correct next token. A loss of 2.0 nats means, on average, the correct token got probability around `e^-2 = 0.135`. Perplexity is `e^loss`.

## Worked example: counting GPT-2 small

GPT-2 small: `L = 12`, `d = 768`, `h = 12`, vocabulary 50,257, context 1,024, learned positions, tied embeddings.

| Component | Formula | Parameters |
|---|---|---|
| Token embedding | V x d = 50,257 x 768 | 38.6M |
| Position embedding | 1,024 x 768 | 0.8M |
| Attention per block | 4 d^2 (Q, K, V, O) | 2.36M |
| MLP per block | 2 x d x 4d = 8 d^2 | 4.72M |
| Per block total (ignoring biases and norms) | 12 d^2 | 7.08M |
| 12 blocks | 12 x 7.08M | 84.9M |
| Total (LM head tied to embedding) | | about 124M |

The rule **parameters per block is about `12 d^2`** (for a 4x MLP and full MHA) is worth memorising. A useful companion rule: a forward pass costs about **`2N` FLOPs per token** (one multiply and one add per weight), so training costs about `6N` per token (forward plus a backward pass that is about twice as expensive).

## Complexity of attention

For sequence length `n` and width `d`:

- Projections and MLP: `O(n d^2)`, linear in sequence length.
- Scores `QK^T` and `weights V`: `O(n^2 d)` time, and naively `O(n^2)` memory per head for the score matrix.

At short contexts the `n d^2` terms dominate; at long contexts the `n^2` terms do. **FlashAttention** does not change the FLOP count; it tiles the computation so the `n x n` matrix never materialises in slow GPU memory (HBM), computing softmax incrementally in fast on-chip SRAM. That cuts memory to `O(n)` and gives large wall-clock speedups because attention is limited by memory bandwidth, not arithmetic.

## A forward pass, step by step, for "The cat sat"

```text
1. tokenize           -> ids [3]
2. embed              -> X [3, d]
3. block 1: norm -> Q,K,V -> RoPE(Q,K) -> masked attention per head -> W_O -> add to X
            norm -> MLP -> add to X
4. blocks 2..L        -> same shape [3, d] throughout
5. final norm, LM head -> logits [3, V]
6. row 2 (after "sat") -> softmax -> " on" with p = 0.4 ...
```

Shapes never change inside the stack: `[T, d]` in, `[T, d]` out. That uniformity is what makes transformers easy to scale by stacking more blocks and widening `d`.

import numpy as np


def softmax(x: np.ndarray, axis: int = -1) -> np.ndarray:
    x = x - x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)  # numerical stability
    e = np.exp(x)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)


def causal_self_attention(x: np.ndarray, w_q, w_k, w_v, w_o, n_heads: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """x: [T, d_model]; w_*: [d_model, d_model]. Returns [T, d_model]."""
    T, d_model = x.shape
    d_head = d_model // n_heads

    def split(m: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:  # [T, d] -> [h, T, d_head]
        return m.reshape(T, n_heads, d_head).transpose(1, 0, 2)

    q, k, v = split(x @ w_q), split(x @ w_k), split(x @ w_v)

    scores = q @ k.transpose(0, 2, 1) / np.sqrt(d_head)        # [h, T, T]
    mask = np.triu(np.ones((T, T), dtype=bool), k=1)           # True above diagonal
    scores = np.where(mask, -np.inf, scores)
    weights = softmax(scores, axis=-1)                         # rows sum to 1

    out = weights @ v                                          # [h, T, d_head]
    out = out.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(T, d_model)           # concat heads
    return out @ w_o


rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
T, d, h = 5, 64, 4
x = rng.standard_normal((T, d))
w = [rng.standard_normal((d, d)) / np.sqrt(d) for _ in range(4)]
y = causal_self_attention(x, *w, n_heads=h)
print(y.shape)  # (5, 64)

# Causality check: changing the last token must not change earlier outputs.
x2 = x.copy()
x2[-1] += 10.0
y2 = causal_self_attention(x2, *w, n_heads=h)
print(np.allclose(y[:-1], y2[:-1]))  # True

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F


def rope(x: torch.Tensor, base: float = 10000.0) -> torch.Tensor:
    """x: [B, h, T, d_head]. Rotates dimension pairs by position-dependent angles."""
    B, h, T, d = x.shape
    inv_freq = base ** (-torch.arange(0, d, 2, device=x.device).float() / d)   # [d/2]
    angles = torch.arange(T, device=x.device).float()[:, None] * inv_freq    # [T, d/2]
    cos, sin = angles.cos(), angles.sin()
    x1, x2 = x[..., 0::2], x[..., 1::2]
    out = torch.stack((x1 * cos - x2 * sin, x1 * sin + x2 * cos), dim=-1)
    return out.flatten(-2)


class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d: int, eps: float = 1e-6):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps, self.weight = eps, nn.Parameter(torch.ones(d))

    def forward(self, x):
        return x * torch.rsqrt(x.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps) * self.weight


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model: int = 512, n_heads: int = 8):
        super().__init__()
        self.h = n_heads
        self.norm1, self.norm2 = RMSNorm(d_model), RMSNorm(d_model)
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model, bias=False)
        self.proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
        hidden = int(8 * d_model / 3)
        self.w_gate = nn.Linear(d_model, hidden, bias=False)
        self.w_up = nn.Linear(d_model, hidden, bias=False)
        self.w_down = nn.Linear(hidden, d_model, bias=False)

    def attention(self, x):
        B, T, D = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).split(D, dim=-1)
        q, k, v = (t.view(B, T, self.h, D // self.h).transpose(1, 2) for t in (q, k, v))
        q, k = rope(q), rope(k)                       # position goes into Q and K only
        y = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)  # fused / flash kernel
        return self.proj(y.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, D))

    def mlp(self, x):
        return self.w_down(F.silu(self.w_gate(x)) * self.w_up(x))  # SwiGLU

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attention(self.norm1(x))   # pre-norm + residual
        x = x + self.mlp(self.norm2(x))
        return x


class TinyLM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab: int = 32000, d_model: int = 512, n_layers: int = 6, n_heads: int = 8):
        super().__init__()
        self.embed = nn.Embedding(vocab, d_model)
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList(Block(d_model, n_heads) for _ in range(n_layers))
        self.norm = RMSNorm(d_model)
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(d_model, vocab, bias=False)

    def forward(self, ids, targets=None):
        x = self.embed(ids)                       # [B, T, d]
        for block in self.blocks:
            x = block(x)
        logits = self.lm_head(self.norm(x))       # [B, T, V]
        loss = None
        if targets is not None:
            loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, logits.size(-1)), targets.view(-1))
        return logits, loss


model = TinyLM()
ids = torch.randint(0, 32000, (2, 16))
logits, loss = model(ids[:, :-1], targets=ids[:, 1:])   # shift by one: predict the next token
print(logits.shape, round(loss.item(), 2))               # [2, 15, 32000], about ln(32000) = 10.4
next_id = logits[:, -1].softmax(-1).multinomial(1)        # sample from the last position only

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

AI-engineer loops rarely ask you to derive backprop, but they do check that you can reason from the architecture to product consequences: why long prompts are slow and expensive, why the model cannot count letters, why context windows have limits, why outputs vary between runs. Expect to whiteboard attention with shapes and to do one piece of arithmetic (parameters, FLOPs or memory).

## Questions with model answers

### 1. Walk me through what happens when an LLM generates the next token.

**Model answer.** The text is tokenised into ids with the model's BPE tokenizer and rendered through its chat template. Ids are looked up in the embedding table to get a `[T, d]` matrix. That flows through `L` transformer blocks; each block applies pre-norm self-attention with a causal mask (tokens mix information from earlier positions only) and a per-position MLP, each added back into the residual stream. After a final norm, the LM head projects the last position's vector to `V` logits. We apply temperature, optionally top-p or top-k, softmax, and sample one id. That id is appended and the loop repeats, reusing cached keys and values so earlier positions are not recomputed.

*What lifts this answer:* mentioning the KV cache, that only the last row of logits is used, and that sampling (not the network) is where randomness comes from.

### 2. Write scaled dot-product attention and explain each term.

**Model answer.** `softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k) + M) V`. `Q`, `K`, `V` are linear projections of the input, shapes `[T, d_k]`, `[T, d_k]`, `[T, d_v]`. `QK^T` is a `[T, T]` matrix of similarity scores. Dividing by `sqrt(d_k)` keeps their variance near 1 so softmax does not saturate. `M` is the causal mask with `-inf` above the diagonal. Softmax over each row gives attention weights that sum to 1, and multiplying by `V` produces each position's weighted mix of values. Multi-head runs this `h` times with `d_k = d_model / h` and concatenates the results through `W_O`.

### 3. Why is attention quadratic, and what do people do about it?

**Model answer.** Every query is scored against every key, so the score matrix is `n x n`: `O(n^2 d)` compute and, naively, `O(n^2)` memory per head. Mitigations fall into groups:

| Approach | Example | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| IO-aware exact kernels | FlashAttention | Same maths, far less memory traffic; still quadratic compute |
| Share K/V across heads | GQA, MQA | Smaller KV cache; slight quality cost |
| Restrict the pattern | Sliding-window attention | Linear cost; distant tokens only reachable via depth |
| Alternative architectures | State-space models, linear attention, hybrids | Linear in length; ecosystem and quality still evolving |

In practice, during decode each new token attends to `n` cached keys, so per-token cost grows linearly with context, and the KV cache grows linearly in memory. That is usually the real bottleneck.

### 4. Why do LLMs struggle to count letters or do long arithmetic?

**Model answer.** The model sees tokens, not characters: `strawberry` may be two or three tokens, and the letters inside are only implicitly represented. Numbers are split into irregular chunks, so digit alignment is not explicit. And a single forward pass has a fixed amount of computation per token, so multi-step algorithms must be spread across generated tokens (chain-of-thought) or delegated to a tool. The product answer is to give the model a calculator or code tool rather than trusting mental arithmetic.

### 5. What is the KV cache and why does causal masking make it possible?

**Model answer.** At each layer, keys and values for past tokens are stored so a new token only computes its own `q`, `k`, `v` and attends to the cached ones. It is valid because of the causal mask: a past token's representation never depends on future tokens, so its keys and values never change when we append. Without the cache, generating `n` tokens would recompute the whole prefix each step. The cost is memory proportional to layers times KV heads times head size times sequence length times batch, which is why GQA matters (covered in the inference lesson).

### 6. Estimate the parameters of a model with 32 layers and d_model = 4096.

**Model answer.** About `12 d^2` per layer: `12 x 4096^2 = 12 x 16.8M = 201M`, times 32 layers is about 6.4B. Add embeddings: with a 32k vocabulary that is `32,000 x 4,096 = 131M`, doubled if the LM head is untied. That lands near 6.7B, which matches Llama 2 7B. The exact split shifts with SwiGLU and GQA, but `12 L d^2` gets you within a few percent and shows you understand where the parameters live.

### 7. Why RoPE instead of learned absolute positions?

**Model answer.** Learned absolute positions give each index its own vector and do not generalise beyond the trained length. RoPE rotates queries and keys so their dot product depends on relative distance, which matches how language works (nearby words matter more), needs no extra parameters, and allows context extension by rescaling rotation frequencies (position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, YaRN) followed by a little long-context fine-tuning. It is not magic: models still degrade past the lengths they were actually trained on.

### 8. Embedding model vs the LLM's token embeddings: same thing?

**Model answer.** No. Token embeddings are the first-layer lookup table, one vector per vocabulary entry, with no context. An embedding model (for search) runs a whole network over a passage and pools the output into one vector, trained contrastively so that related texts are close. You use the latter for retrieval; the former is an internal detail.

## Common mistakes

- Saying attention is `O(n^2)` without saying in *what* (compute and naive memory) and without mentioning that decode is linear per token with a cache.
- Forgetting the causal mask, or putting `-inf` on the wrong side of the diagonal.
- Applying RoPE to values.
- Claiming temperature 0 is fully deterministic: batching and floating-point non-associativity on GPUs can still change outputs.
- Measuring prompt size with characters instead of the provider's tokenizer.

## Quick numbers to have ready

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| Parameters per block | about 12 d^2 |
| Forward FLOPs per token | about 2N |
| Training FLOPs per token | about 6N |
| English characters per token | roughly 4 |
| Attention score matrix | n x n per head |

Byte-level BPE builds subword tokens from frequent merges; costs, limits and quirks like letter counting follow from it.
Attention is softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k) + causal mask) V; multi-head runs many small attentions in parallel.
Each block is pre-norm attention plus a per-position MLP, both added into the residual stream; shapes stay [T, d].
RoPE rotates queries and keys so attention depends on relative position; it is the default in open models.
Rules of thumb: about 12 d^2 parameters per block, 2N FLOPs per token forward, 6N per token for training.

options: To normalise the rows so they sum to 1
To make attention linear in sequence length
To keep dot-product variance near 1 so softmax does not saturate
To encode token position
check.why: Dot products of d_k unit-variance components have variance d_k; scaling restores unit variance and keeps gradients alive. Softmax, not the scaling, makes rows sum to 1.

options: The same size
One quarter the size
One eighth the size
Four times larger
check.why: Grouped-query attention stores K and V only for the 8 KV heads, so the cache is 8/32 = 1/4 of the MHA cache.

check.q: What makes it valid to cache keys and values of earlier tokens during generation?
options: RoPE makes positions relative
Layer norm keeps activations stable
The MLP is applied per position
The causal mask means earlier positions never depend on later tokens
check.why: With causal masking, appending tokens cannot change any earlier position's hidden states, so their keys and values can be reused.

lessons.summary: Pretraining data and scaling laws, SFT, RLHF and DPO, benchmarks, why models hallucinate, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning with LoRA and QLoRA.

parts.label: Concepts
parts.body:
## The pipeline at a glance

A modern chat model is built in stages. Each stage uses a different kind of data and changes the model in a different way.

```text
raw web + code + books ...  --pretraining-->  base model (predicts text, not helpful)
demonstrations (prompt, ideal response) --SFT-->  instruction-following model
preference pairs / verifiable rewards  --RLHF, DPO, RL-->  aligned assistant / reasoning model
your domain data (optional)  --fine-tune (LoRA)-->  specialised model
```

Almost all the knowledge and capability comes from pretraining. Post-training shapes behaviour: format, tone, refusal, tool use and, increasingly, step-by-step reasoning.

## Pretraining

### Objective

Next-token prediction with cross-entropy loss, over trillions of tokens. For a sequence `x_1..x_T` the loss is the average of `-log P(x_t | x_<t)`. Because of the causal mask, one forward pass trains every position at once.

Nothing in this objective says "be truthful" or "be helpful". The model learns whatever statistics make the next token predictable: grammar, facts, code structure, reasoning patterns, and also errors and biases in the data.

### Data

Pretraining corpora are mixtures: filtered web crawls (Common Crawl derivatives), code, books, papers, maths, multilingual text, and increasingly synthetic data generated by earlier models. The hard engineering is in the pipeline, not the model:

| Step | Why |
|---|---|
| Text extraction from HTML/PDF | Boilerplate and broken markup waste tokens |
| Language identification and quality filtering | Classifier or heuristic filters remove spam and junk |
| Deduplication (exact and near-duplicate, e.g. MinHash) | Duplicates cause memorisation and waste compute |
| PII and toxicity filtering | Safety and privacy |
| Benchmark decontamination | Keep test sets out so evaluations stay meaningful |
| Mixture weighting and annealing | Upweight high-quality code/maths, often more of it near the end of training |

Open datasets such as FineWeb (Hugging Face) document these steps in public and are a good reference for how much filtering matters.

### Compute and scaling laws

Training compute is approximately:

```text
C  ~=  6 * N * D       (FLOPs)
N = parameters, D = training tokens
```

Kaplan et al. (2020) showed loss falls as a smooth power law in `N`, `D` and `C`. Hoffmann et al. (2022, "Chinchilla") revisited the allocation and found that for a fixed compute budget, parameters and tokens should grow roughly in proportion, about **20 tokens per parameter**. Their 70B Chinchilla model, trained on 1.4T tokens, outperformed the 280B Gopher trained with the same compute.

Since then, labs deliberately **over-train** smaller models far past 20 tokens per parameter (Meta reported training Llama 3 on over 15T tokens). Chinchilla optimises training compute; a model that will serve billions of requests should optimise *total* cost, and a smaller model trained longer is cheaper at inference.

### Worked example: what does training a 7B model cost?

```text
N = 7e9 parameters, D = 2e12 tokens
C = 6 * 7e9 * 2e12 = 8.4e22 FLOPs

Assume each GPU sustains 400 TFLOP/s of useful work (a plausible
fraction of a modern accelerator's dense BF16 peak; measure MFU in practice):
GPU-seconds = 8.4e22 / 4e14 = 2.1e8 s  ->  about 58,000 GPU-hours
On 1,024 GPUs: about 57 hours of pure compute, before failures and restarts.
```

This is why only a handful of organisations pretrain frontier models, and why most product teams start from an existing base or instruct model.

### Memory during training

With mixed precision and Adam, a common estimate is about **16 bytes per parameter** before activations: 2 for BF16 weights, 2 for gradients, and 12 for the FP32 master weights plus Adam's two moment estimates. A 7B model therefore needs about 112 GB just for state, more than one 80 GB GPU, which is why training uses sharding (ZeRO/FSDP), tensor and pipeline parallelism, and activation checkpointing.

## Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)

A base model continues text. Ask it a question and it may produce more questions. SFT trains on curated `(prompt, response)` pairs rendered through a chat template, with loss computed **only on the response tokens** (prompt tokens are masked out). Tens of thousands of high-quality examples can change behaviour dramatically because the knowledge is already there; SFT teaches the format and the persona.

Quality beats quantity here. Inconsistent or low-quality demonstrations teach inconsistency. SFT data increasingly includes tool-call traces, multi-turn conversations and reasoning traces.

## RLHF: learning from preferences

It is easier for people to compare two answers than to write a perfect one. RLHF, popularised by InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., 2022), uses comparisons:

1. **Collect preferences.** For a prompt, sample several responses; labellers rank them.
2. **Train a reward model.** A copy of the LM with a scalar head is trained so the preferred response scores higher, with a Bradley-Terry loss: `-log sigmoid(r(x, y_win) - r(x, y_lose))`.
3. **Optimise the policy with RL** (PPO in InstructGPT) to maximise reward, minus a **KL penalty** that keeps it close to the SFT model:

```text
objective = E[ r(x, y) ] - beta * KL( pi_theta(y|x) || pi_ref(y|x) )
```

Without the KL term, the policy finds outputs that fool the reward model (**reward hacking**): verbose, sycophantic or oddly formatted text that scores well but is not better. InstructGPT reported that outputs of its 1.3B model were preferred by labellers over the 175B GPT-3, a striking demonstration that alignment can matter more than size for usefulness.

PPO-based RLHF is powerful but complex: it keeps the policy, a reference model, a reward model and a value model in memory and is sensitive to hyperparameters.

## DPO: preferences without a reward model

Direct Preference Optimization (Rafailov et al., 2023) shows that the KL-constrained RLHF objective has a closed-form optimal policy, and rearranges it into a simple classification loss on preference pairs:

```text
L_DPO = -log sigmoid( beta * [ log pi(y_w|x)/pi_ref(y_w|x)  -  log pi(y_l|x)/pi_ref(y_l|x) ] )
```

It increases the likelihood of the chosen response relative to the reference model and decreases that of the rejected one. No reward model, no sampling during training, just two forward passes per pair. That simplicity made DPO and its variants very popular for open models.

| | RLHF with PPO | DPO |
|---|---|---|
| Needs reward model | Yes | No (implicit) |
| Samples from policy during training | Yes (on-policy) | No (offline pairs) |
| Models in memory | Policy, reference, reward, value | Policy, reference |
| Stability and cost | Harder, costlier | Simpler, cheaper |
| Weakness | Reward hacking, tuning effort | Limited by the fixed dataset; can over-optimise |

## RL for reasoning

Since 2024, a major thread is reinforcement learning with **verifiable rewards**: maths answers that can be checked, code that must pass tests. The model generates long chains of reasoning and is rewarded for correct final answers. DeepSeek's papers describe GRPO, a PPO variant that drops the value model and compares a group of sampled answers to each other, and DeepSeek-R1 reported that strong reasoning behaviour can emerge from this kind of RL. The details of frontier labs' recipes are not public; treat specific claims about them with care.

The result is "reasoning" or "thinking" models that spend more tokens at inference time before answering. That is a cost and latency trade-off you will meet again in the serving and production lessons.

code.source:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def sequence_logprob(model, input_ids: torch.Tensor, labels: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Sum of log P(token) over response tokens (labels == -100 are ignored). Returns [B]."""
    logits = model(input_ids).logits[:, :-1]          # predict token t+1 from prefix up to t
    targets = labels[:, 1:]
    mask = targets != -100
    logp = torch.log_softmax(logits.float(), dim=-1)
    picked = logp.gather(-1, targets.clamp(min=0).unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1)
    return (picked * mask).sum(-1)


def reward_model_loss(r_chosen: torch.Tensor, r_rejected: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Bradley-Terry loss used to train an RLHF reward model."""
    return -F.logsigmoid(r_chosen - r_rejected).mean()


def dpo_loss(policy, reference, batch, beta: float = 0.1):
    """batch holds tokenised chosen/rejected sequences for the same prompts."""
    pi_w = sequence_logprob(policy, batch["chosen_ids"], batch["chosen_labels"])
    pi_l = sequence_logprob(policy, batch["rejected_ids"], batch["rejected_labels"])
    with torch.no_grad():                               # reference model is frozen
        ref_w = sequence_logprob(reference, batch["chosen_ids"], batch["chosen_labels"])
        ref_l = sequence_logprob(reference, batch["rejected_ids"], batch["rejected_labels"])

    margin = beta * ((pi_w - ref_w) - (pi_l - ref_l))
    loss = -F.logsigmoid(margin).mean()
    metrics = {
        "reward_accuracy": (margin > 0).float().mean().item(),   # chosen beats rejected
        "chosen_reward": (beta * (pi_w - ref_w)).mean().item(),
        "rejected_reward": (beta * (pi_l - ref_l)).mean().item(),
    }
    return loss, metrics

parts.body:
## Evaluation and benchmarks

How do you know a model is good? Three families of evidence, each with blind spots.

| Kind | Examples | Measures | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Static benchmarks | MMLU (knowledge), GSM8K and MATH (maths), HumanEval (code), GPQA (hard science QA) | Accuracy on fixed questions | Saturation, contamination (test items in training data), prompt-format sensitivity |
| Agentic / realistic tasks | SWE-bench (fix real GitHub issues), web and tool-use suites | End-to-end task success | Harness differences make cross-paper comparisons unreliable |
| Human preference | LMArena (formerly Chatbot Arena): blind pairwise votes, Elo-style ratings | What users prefer in open chat | Style and length bias; not your use case |

The practical lesson for engineers: **public benchmarks pick a shortlist; your own eval set picks the model.** A model that tops a leaderboard can still fail your extraction format or your domain vocabulary. The evals lesson later in the course builds that eval set.

Perplexity (exponentiated loss on held-out text) is the core pretraining metric, but it says little about instruction following or safety and is not comparable across tokenizers.

## Why models hallucinate

A hallucination is fluent output that is not supported by facts or by the provided context. It follows from how models are built:

1. **The objective rewards plausibility, not truth.** Pretraining maximises the probability of text that *looks like* the corpus. A confident, well-formed wrong answer is often highly probable.
2. **Knowledge is lossy and long-tailed.** Facts seen once or twice (a minor person's birthday, an obscure API flag) are stored weakly. The model still produces *something* in the right shape.
3. **There is no built-in "I don't know".** Unless post-training rewards abstaining, guessing scores better than refusing on most benchmarks, so models learn to guess.
4. **Knowledge has a cutoff** and the model cannot see the clock unless you tell it.
5. **Decoding can amplify errors.** Once a wrong token is sampled, later tokens condition on it and rationalise it.

Mitigations, in rough order of effectiveness for products:

| Mitigation | Why it helps |
|---|---|
| Ground with retrieval (RAG) and require citations | Moves the task from recall to reading |
| Give tools for facts and arithmetic | Calculators, search, databases are exact |
| Allow and reward abstention in the prompt and the eval | "If the context does not contain the answer, say so" |
| Constrain output (schemas, enums) | Less room to invent |
| Verify after generation (citation checks, a second model, rules) | Catches some errors before the user does |
| Lower temperature for factual tasks | Reduces sampling of unlikely tokens, not knowledge gaps |

No mitigation drives the rate to zero. Design the UX so wrong answers are recoverable: show sources, let users check.

## Fine-tuning: when and how

Reach for fine-tuning *after* prompting and retrieval, when you need:

- A consistent output format or style that prompts cannot reliably enforce.
- Lower latency or cost by distilling a big model's behaviour into a small one.
- Domain-specific behaviour (classification labels, a house writing style).

Do **not** fine-tune to add facts that change; that is retrieval's job. Fine-tuned facts are hard to update, hard to cite and still hallucinated at the edges.

### Full fine-tuning vs parameter-efficient

Full fine-tuning updates every weight and needs the 16 bytes per parameter of optimiser state discussed earlier. **LoRA** (Hu et al., 2021) freezes the base weights and learns a low-rank update for selected matrices:

```text
W' = W + (alpha / r) * B A
W: [d, k] frozen     B: [d, r] (init zeros)     A: [r, k] (init random)
r is small: 8, 16, 32, 64
```

Because `B` starts at zero, the model starts exactly at the base model. Only `A` and `B` are trained.

**Worked example.** One `4096 x 4096` projection has 16.8M weights. LoRA with `r = 16` adds `16 x (4096 + 4096) = 131,072` trainable parameters, about 0.8% of that matrix. Applied to the Q, K, V and O projections of 32 layers: `4 x 32 x 131,072 = 16.8M` trainable parameters for a 7B model, so optimiser state is tiny and adapters are a few tens of MB on disk. The LoRA paper reported, for GPT-3 175B, cutting trainable parameters by about 10,000x and GPU memory by about 3x versus full fine-tuning, with comparable quality on its tasks.

Practical properties:

- Adapters can be **merged** into `W` for zero extra inference latency, or kept separate so one server hosts many adapters over one base model (vLLM and others support multi-LoRA serving).
- Which matrices to target matters. Targeting all linear layers (attention and MLP) usually beats attention-only at the same budget.
- `alpha / r` scales the update; a common starting point is `alpha = 2r`.

### QLoRA

QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) keeps the frozen base model in **4-bit** precision (the NF4 data type, plus double quantisation of the scaling constants) and trains LoRA adapters in 16-bit on top, with paged optimisers to absorb memory spikes. The paper fine-tuned a 65B model on a single 48 GB GPU. The cost is slower steps (dequantising on the fly) and a small quality gap that is often negligible.

### Memory comparison for a 7B model (approximate, excluding activations)

| Method | Weights | Trainable state | Rough total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full fine-tune (BF16 + Adam) | 14 GB | about 98 GB | about 112 GB |
| LoRA on BF16 base | 14 GB | under 1 GB | about 15 GB |
| QLoRA on 4-bit base | about 4 GB | under 1 GB | about 5 GB |

Activations add more, depending on batch size and sequence length; gradient checkpointing trades compute to reduce them.

## A sane fine-tuning workflow

1. Write the eval first: 100 to 500 held-out examples with a scoring rule.
2. Baseline with the best prompt (and few-shot examples) on candidate models.
3. Build training data in the exact chat template the model expects; mask the prompt from the loss.
4. Start with LoRA, `r = 16`, all linear layers, 1 to 3 epochs, learning rate around `1e-4` to `2e-4`. Watch validation loss for overfitting.
5. Evaluate on the held-out set *and* a general regression set, since fine-tuning can erode general skills (catastrophic forgetting) and safety behaviour.
6. Version the dataset, the base model and the adapter together.

Hosted APIs also offer fine-tuning (supervised and, on some platforms, preference-based) without managing GPUs; the same evaluation discipline applies.

# QLoRA fine-tuning sketch with Hugging Face transformers + peft + bitsandbytes.
# Conceptual: pin versions and check each library's docs before running for real.
import torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model, prepare_model_for_kbit_training
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, BitsAndBytesConfig

BASE = "your-org/your-base-instruct-model"   # any causal LM on the Hub you are licensed to use

bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(
    load_in_4bit=True,
    bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",            # NormalFloat4 from the QLoRA paper
    bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,       # quantise the quantisation constants too
    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BASE)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(BASE, quantization_config=bnb, device_map="auto")
model = prepare_model_for_kbit_training(model)   # enables gradient checkpointing, casts norms

lora = LoraConfig(
    r=16,
    lora_alpha=32,
    lora_dropout=0.05,
    target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj", "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"],
    task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
)
model = get_peft_model(model, lora)
model.print_trainable_parameters()   # e.g. "trainable params: ~40M || all params: ~8B || trainable%: ~0.5"


def to_features(example):
    """Render with the model's own chat template and mask the prompt from the loss."""
    prompt = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
        [{"role": "user", "content": example["prompt"]}], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True
    )
    full = prompt + example["response"] + tokenizer.eos_token
    ids = tokenizer(full, truncation=True, max_length=2048)["input_ids"]
    n_prompt = len(tokenizer(prompt)["input_ids"])
    labels = [-100] * n_prompt + ids[n_prompt:]      # -100 = ignored by cross-entropy
    return {"input_ids": ids, "labels": labels}


data = load_dataset("json", data_files={"train": "train.jsonl", "eval": "eval.jsonl"})
data = data.map(to_features, remove_columns=data["train"].column_names)

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

For AI-engineer roles the questions are about judgement: when to prompt vs retrieve vs fine-tune, what alignment does and does not fix, how to read a benchmark claim, and whether you can estimate compute and memory. For research-adjacent roles expect to write the DPO or reward-model loss.

## Questions with model answers

### 1. Explain the stages that turn a base model into a chat assistant.

**Model answer.** Pretraining on trillions of tokens with next-token prediction gives a base model that knows a lot but just continues text. Supervised fine-tuning on curated prompt-response pairs, rendered in a chat template and with loss only on responses, teaches it to follow instructions and adopt a format. Preference optimisation (RLHF with a reward model and PPO, or DPO directly on preference pairs) pushes it toward responses people prefer: more helpful, more honest about uncertainty, safer. Newer models add RL on verifiable tasks (maths, code tests) to improve multi-step reasoning. Capabilities come mostly from pretraining; post-training shapes behaviour.

### 2. RLHF vs DPO: what is the difference and when would you pick each?

**Model answer.** Both optimise a policy to prefer chosen over rejected responses while staying close to a reference model. RLHF trains an explicit reward model, then uses on-policy RL (PPO) with a KL penalty; it can keep improving as the policy explores, but it needs four models in memory, is finicky, and invites reward hacking. DPO derives a closed-form loss directly on preference pairs: no reward model, no sampling, two forward passes per example. For a product team with a fixed preference dataset, DPO is the pragmatic default. On-policy RL is worth it when you have a good reward signal you can query repeatedly, such as unit tests or a verifier.

### 3. What do scaling laws tell you, and why are models trained far beyond Chinchilla-optimal?

**Model answer.** Loss falls predictably as a power law in parameters, data and compute, so labs can forecast a large run from small ones. Chinchilla found that for fixed training compute you should scale parameters and tokens together, about 20 tokens per parameter. But that minimises *training* cost. Serving cost scales with parameter count for every token ever generated, so it pays to train a smaller model on many more tokens; it is slightly less compute-efficient to train but much cheaper to run. Hence 8B-class models trained on 15T+ tokens.

### 4. Estimate the compute to train a 13B model on 3T tokens.

**Model answer.** `C = 6ND = 6 x 13e9 x 3e12 = 2.34e23` FLOPs. At an assumed 400 TFLOP/s sustained per GPU that is `2.34e23 / 4e14 = 5.85e8` GPU-seconds, about 160,000 GPU-hours, or roughly a week on 1,000 GPUs ignoring failures. I would state the utilisation assumption explicitly because it can easily vary by 2x.

### 5. A stakeholder wants to fine-tune a model on the company wiki so it "knows" internal docs. What do you advise?

**Model answer.** Start with retrieval, not fine-tuning. Docs change weekly; fine-tuned knowledge is frozen, cannot cite sources, and is still hallucinated at the edges. RAG keeps answers current, traceable and permission-aware (you can filter by who may see what). Fine-tuning is the right tool if, after RAG, we still need a consistent format, a house tone, or to distil a large model into a cheaper one, and I would prove the gain against an eval set before and after.

### 6. How does LoRA work and why is it so memory-efficient?

**Model answer.** It freezes the pretrained weight `W` and learns a low-rank update `BA`, with `B` of shape `d x r` initialised to zero and `A` of shape `r x k`, scaled by `alpha / r`. With `r = 16` on a `4096 x 4096` matrix that is 131k trainable parameters instead of 16.8M. Gradients and Adam state exist only for adapters, so optimiser memory nearly disappears; the frozen base can even be quantised to 4-bit (QLoRA). Adapters can be merged for zero inference overhead or swapped per tenant on one base model.

### 7. Why do models hallucinate, and what would you do about it in a product?

**Model answer.** The training objective rewards plausible continuations, long-tail facts are stored weakly, and evaluation and post-training have historically rewarded guessing over abstaining. In a product I would ground answers in retrieved sources with citations, give tools for exact facts, explicitly allow "I don't know" and score it as acceptable in evals, constrain outputs with schemas, and add a verification step for high-stakes outputs. Then design the UI so users can check sources. I would not claim any of this eliminates hallucination.

### 8. A vendor says their model scores 90% on MMLU. How much weight do you give that?

**Model answer.** Some, for shortlisting. I would ask about contamination checks, the prompt format and number of shots, and whether the number is comparable to others' reported numbers. MMLU is near saturation for frontier models, so differences at the top are small and noisy. The decision comes from our own eval set on our tasks, plus latency and cost measured on our traffic.

## Common mistakes

- Treating fine-tuning as the way to add knowledge.
- Forgetting to mask prompt tokens from the SFT loss, or training with a different chat template than inference uses.
- Describing RLHF without the KL penalty, and so missing reward hacking.
- Quoting benchmark numbers as if they were universal truths.
- Ignoring catastrophic forgetting: evaluate general skills after fine-tuning, not only the target task.

## Formulas to have ready

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| Training compute | C = 6ND |
| Chinchilla rule of thumb | D is about 20N |
| Adam mixed-precision state | about 16 bytes per parameter |
| LoRA params per matrix | r (d + k) |
| Reward model loss | -log sigmoid(r_w - r_l) |
| DPO loss | -log sigmoid(beta [(log-ratio chosen) - (log-ratio rejected)]) |

keyPoints: Pretraining with next-token prediction supplies almost all knowledge; post-training shapes behaviour and format.
Training compute is about 6ND; Chinchilla suggests about 20 tokens per parameter, but models are over-trained to cut serving cost.
SFT teaches instruction following from demonstrations, with loss masked to the response tokens.
RLHF trains a reward model and optimises with PPO under a KL penalty; DPO gets a similar effect with a simple loss on pairs.
Hallucination follows from a plausibility objective and guess-rewarding evals; ground, cite, allow abstention and verify.
Use LoRA/QLoRA for format, style or distillation, not for facts that change; always evaluate before and after.

check.q: Why do labs train small models on far more than 20 tokens per parameter?
options: Chinchilla was shown to be wrong
Serving cost scales with model size, so a smaller model trained longer is cheaper overall
More tokens reduce hallucination to zero
Larger vocabularies require more tokens
check.why: Chinchilla minimises training compute. Total cost includes inference on every request, which favours smaller, longer-trained models.

check.q: What role does the KL penalty play in RLHF?
options: It speeds up PPO convergence
It replaces the reward model
It normalises the reward scale across prompts
It keeps the policy close to the reference model and limits reward hacking
check.why: Without it the policy drifts toward outputs that exploit reward-model flaws rather than genuinely better responses.

check.q: A LoRA adapter with r = 8 is applied to a 4096 x 4096 matrix. How many trainable parameters does it add?
check.why: B is 4096 x 8 and A is 8 x 4096, so r (d + k) = 8 x 8192 = 65,536 parameters.

## Two phases: prefill and decode

Every generation request runs in two very different phases.

```text
prompt (2,000 tokens) --PREFILL--> KV cache for 2,000 tokens + first output token
                      --DECODE---> token 2, token 3, ... one forward pass per token
```

| | Prefill | Decode |
|---|---|---|
| Work | All prompt tokens in one parallel forward pass | One new token per forward pass |
| Bottleneck | Compute (big matrix-matrix multiplies) | Memory bandwidth (read all weights and the KV cache for each token) |
| Drives | Time to first token (TTFT) | Time per output token (TPOT) |
| Scales with | Prompt length (attention part quadratically) | Output length times context length |

The key insight: in decode with batch size 1, the GPU reads every weight from memory to do about 2 FLOPs per weight. Arithmetic intensity is tiny, so the GPU's compute units mostly wait on memory. **Batching** many sequences shares each weight read across many tokens, which is why serving throughput depends so much on batch size.

### Back-of-envelope decode speed

```text
8B model in BF16 = 16 GB of weights
GPU memory bandwidth (H100-class HBM) ~ 3 TB/s
Lower bound per token at batch 1 = 16 GB / 3 TB/s ~ 5.3 ms  ->  at most ~190 tokens/s
```

Real numbers are lower (kernel overheads, KV reads), but this bound explains why quantising weights to 8 or 4 bits speeds decode up almost proportionally: fewer bytes to read per token.

## The KV cache

During decode, each layer needs the keys and values of every previous token. Recomputing them would make generation quadratic, so they are cached.

### Memory formula

```text
bytes per token = 2 (K and V) x n_layers x n_kv_heads x head_dim x bytes_per_value
total           = bytes per token x sequence length x batch size
```

### Worked example 1: Llama 2 7B (full multi-head attention)

```text
n_layers = 32, n_kv_heads = 32, head_dim = 128, FP16 (2 bytes)
per token = 2 x 32 x 32 x 128 x 2 = 524,288 bytes = 0.5 MiB
4,096-token sequence  -> 2 GiB
batch of 16           -> 32 GiB, more than double the 13.5 GB of weights
```

### Worked example 2: Llama 3 8B (grouped-query attention, 8 KV heads)

```text
per token = 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB
8,192-token sequence  -> 1 GiB
On an 80 GB GPU: 80 - 16 (weights) - ~4 (activations, overhead) = ~60 GB for KV
-> about 60 concurrent 8k-token sequences, or 480 at 1k tokens each
```

Two takeaways. First, the **KV cache, not the weights, limits concurrency** at long contexts. Second, architectural choices like GQA (4x smaller cache here) and **FP8 KV cache** (another 2x) translate directly into more concurrent users per GPU and lower cost per token.

### Prefix (prompt) caching

If many requests share a prefix (a long system prompt, a tool schema, a document), the server can keep that prefix's KV cache and skip its prefill. vLLM's automatic prefix caching and SGLang's RadixAttention do this on self-hosted servers. Hosted APIs expose the same idea as **prompt caching** with discounted pricing for cached input tokens. Put stable content first and variable content last to benefit.

## Sampling: turning logits into a token

The model outputs logits. How you pick from them changes quality, diversity and determinism.

| Strategy | What it does | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| Greedy | Always the highest-probability token | Short deterministic outputs; can loop or be bland on long text |
| Temperature T | Divide logits by T before softmax. T < 1 sharpens, T > 1 flattens | 0 to 0.3 for extraction and code, 0.7 to 1.0 for creative text |
| Top-k | Keep the k most likely tokens, renormalise | Crude cutoff of the long tail |
| Top-p (nucleus) | Keep the smallest set whose probability sums to p (e.g. 0.9) | Adapts to how confident the model is |
| Min-p | Keep tokens with probability at least `min_p x p_max` | Popular in open-model serving; scales with confidence |
| Repetition / frequency / presence penalties | Down-weight tokens already generated | Reduce loops |
| Beam search | Track the best k partial sequences | Translation-style tasks; rarely used for chat |
| Constrained / structured decoding | Mask tokens that would violate a grammar or JSON schema | Guaranteed-parseable JSON, enums, tool arguments |

Order matters in implementations: typically penalties, then temperature, then truncation (top-k, top-p), then sample. Note that **reasoning models often fix or restrict sampling parameters** in hosted APIs; check the provider's docs instead of assuming temperature is available.

### Worked example

```text
logits:  " mat" 3.0   " floor" 2.0   " roof" 1.0   " moon" -1.0
T = 1.0: softmax -> 0.66, 0.24, 0.09, 0.01
T = 0.5: logits / 0.5 = 6, 4, 2, -2 -> 0.87, 0.12, 0.02, 0.0003
top-p 0.85 at T = 1: " mat" (0.66) is not enough; adding " floor" (0.24) reaches 0.90
                     -> keep those two, renormalise to 0.73, 0.27
```

### Determinism caveat

Temperature 0 (greedy) is not a guarantee of identical outputs across calls. Batched GPU kernels can sum floating-point numbers in different orders depending on what else is in the batch, which can flip a near-tie between two tokens. If you need reproducibility, log outputs rather than assuming you can regenerate them.

## Structured output

Asking nicely for JSON fails some fraction of the time. Robust options:

1. **Provider structured outputs** with a JSON Schema (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and others offer variants) that constrain decoding.
2. **Grammar-constrained decoding** when self-hosting (vLLM supports guided decoding backends; libraries like Outlines and XGrammar implement it).
3. Always **validate** the result (zod, Pydantic) and retry or fall back on failure. Constrained decoding guarantees syntax, not that the values are correct.

import numpy as np


def sample_next(
    logits: np.ndarray,
    generated: list[int],
    temperature: float = 0.8,
    top_k: int | None = None,
    top_p: float | None = 0.95,
    min_p: float | None = None,
    repetition_penalty: float = 1.0,
    rng: np.random.Generator | None = None,
) -> int:
    """Pick the next token id from a [V] logits vector."""
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    logits = logits.astype(np.float64).copy()

    # 1. Repetition penalty (CTRL-style): make already-used tokens less likely.
    if repetition_penalty != 1.0 and generated:
        used = np.unique(generated)
        logits[used] = np.where(logits[used] > 0, logits[used] / repetition_penalty, logits[used] * repetition_penalty)

    # 2. Greedy shortcut.
    if temperature <= 0:
        return int(np.argmax(logits))

    # 3. Temperature, then softmax.
    logits /= temperature
    probs = np.exp(logits - logits.max())
    probs /= probs.sum()

    # 4. Truncation filters.
    keep = np.ones_like(probs, dtype=bool)
    if top_k is not None:
        kth = np.sort(probs)[-top_k]
        keep &= probs >= kth
    if min_p is not None:
        keep &= probs >= min_p * probs.max()
    if top_p is not None:
        order = np.argsort(-probs)
        cumulative = np.cumsum(probs[order])
        cutoff = np.searchsorted(cumulative, top_p) + 1      # smallest prefix reaching top_p
        nucleus = np.zeros_like(keep)
        nucleus[order[:cutoff]] = True
        keep &= nucleus

    probs = np.where(keep, probs, 0.0)
    probs /= probs.sum()
    return int(rng.choice(len(probs), p=probs))


logits = np.array([3.0, 2.0, 1.0, -1.0])     # " mat", " floor", " roof", " moon"
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
picks = [sample_next(logits, [], temperature=1.0, top_p=0.85, rng=rng) for _ in range(1000)]
print(np.bincount(picks, minlength=4) / 1000)   # about [0.73, 0.27, 0, 0]


def kv_cache_bytes(layers: int, kv_heads: int, head_dim: int, seq_len: int, batch: int, bytes_per: int = 2) -> int:
    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * bytes_per * seq_len * batch


GiB = 1024**3
print(kv_cache_bytes(32, 32, 128, 4096, 1) / GiB)   # Llama-2-7B-like, MHA: 2.0 GiB
print(kv_cache_bytes(32, 8, 128, 8192, 1) / GiB)    # Llama-3-8B-like, GQA: 1.0 GiB

## Batching

### Static batching

Collect N requests, run them together until *all* finish. Short requests sit idle waiting for the longest; new arrivals wait for the whole batch. GPU utilisation is poor for chat traffic, where output lengths vary from 5 to 2,000 tokens.

### Continuous (iteration-level) batching

Introduced by the Orca system (OSDI 2022) and now standard in vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM and Hugging Face TGI. The scheduler re-forms the batch **every decode step**: finished sequences leave immediately, waiting requests join as soon as there is memory.

```text
step:      1  2  3  4  5  6  7  8
req A:     a  a  a  a  .            (finished, slot freed)
req B:     b  b  b  b  b  b  b  b
req C:        c  c  c               (joined at step 2)
req D:                 d  d  d  d   (takes A's slot at step 5)
```

Prefill of new requests competes with decode of running ones. **Chunked prefill** splits long prompts into pieces interleaved with decode steps so a 50k-token prompt does not stall everyone else's streaming. Some large deployments go further and run prefill and decode on separate GPU pools (**disaggregated serving**), since they have different bottlenecks.

## PagedAttention and vLLM

Before vLLM, servers pre-allocated a contiguous KV buffer per request sized for the maximum length. Most of it went unused, and fragmentation wasted more. The vLLM paper (Kwon et al., 2023) reported that existing systems wasted a large share of KV memory this way (60 to 80% in their measurements).

**PagedAttention** borrows virtual memory from operating systems:

```text
logical KV blocks for request A:  [0][1][2]        block = 16 tokens
block table A:                    0->7, 1->2, 2->9
physical GPU blocks:  [ ][ ][A1][ ][ ][ ][ ][A0][ ][A2] ...
```

- KV memory is split into fixed-size blocks (16 tokens by default in vLLM).
- Each sequence has a block table mapping logical to physical blocks, allocated on demand.
- Waste is limited to the last partial block of each sequence.
- Blocks can be **shared** with copy-on-write: parallel samples of one prompt, beam search and prefix caching reuse the same physical blocks.

Less waste means bigger batches, and bigger batches mean higher throughput. The paper reported 2 to 4x throughput over prior systems at similar latency. vLLM also provides an OpenAI-compatible HTTP server, so apps can switch between hosted and self-hosted models by changing a base URL.

## Quantisation

Store weights (and optionally activations and KV cache) in fewer bits.

| Format | Bytes per param | 8B weights | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| FP32 | 4 | 32 GB | Training master weights only |
| BF16 / FP16 | 2 | 16 GB | Default serving precision |
| FP8 | 1 | 8 GB | Hardware support on recent NVIDIA (Hopper and later) and others; usually small quality loss |
| INT8 (e.g. LLM.int8, SmoothQuant) | 1 | 8 GB | Outlier handling matters |
| INT4 (GPTQ, AWQ) / GGUF Q4 variants | about 0.5 | about 4.5 GB | Weight-only; good for decode-bound and local serving |

Methods differ in how they pick scales: **GPTQ** uses approximate second-order information to minimise layer output error; **AWQ** protects the weight channels that matter most for activations. Weight-only quantisation mainly speeds up memory-bound decode; it helps prefill less, since dequantisation costs compute. Always evaluate the quantised model on *your* tasks: average benchmark loss may be small while specific skills (maths, long-context retrieval, non-English) degrade more.

## Speculative decoding

Decode is memory-bound, so verifying several tokens in one forward pass costs about the same as generating one. Speculative decoding exploits this:

1. A cheap **draft** (a small model, extra prediction heads as in Medusa or EAGLE, or n-gram lookup from the prompt) proposes k tokens.
2. The large **target** model scores all k positions in one forward pass.
3. Accept the longest prefix consistent with the target using a rejection-sampling rule, then add one token from the target.

With the rejection-sampling scheme from Leviathan et al. and Chen et al., the output distribution is **exactly** the target model's. The speedup depends on the acceptance rate: high for predictable text (code, structured output, summaries that copy the input), low for creative text. It helps latency most at low batch sizes; at very high batch sizes the GPU is already busy and gains shrink.

## Latency metrics

| Metric | Definition | What drives it |
|---|---|---|
| TTFT (time to first token) | Request arrival to first streamed token | Queueing, prefill length, prefix cache hits |
| TPOT / ITL (time per output token, inter-token latency) | Average gap between streamed tokens | Model size, batch size, quantisation, speculative decoding |
| End-to-end latency | TTFT + TPOT x (output tokens - 1) | Both, plus output length |
| Throughput | Output tokens per second across all requests | Batch size, KV memory |
| Goodput | Requests per second that meet the latency SLO | The metric to optimise in production |

Report **percentiles** (p50, p95, p99), not averages. A useful reading speed reference: people read a few words per second, so a TPOT of 20 to 50 ms already streams faster than anyone reads; TTFT is what users perceive as "slow".

Throughput and latency trade off directly: bigger batches raise throughput and cost efficiency but raise TPOT for everyone. The serving config is a choice on that curve.

## Self-hosting vs API: a cost model

There is no universal answer, so reason with a formula instead of a quote.

```text
self-hosted cost per 1M output tokens =
    GPU $/hour / (tokens per second x 3600) x 1,000,000 / utilisation
```

**Illustrative example** (assumed numbers, replace with current prices and your benchmark):

```text
GPU rental: $2.50 / hour
Measured aggregate throughput for your model and traffic: 2,500 output tokens/s
At 100% utilisation: 2.50 / (2,500 x 3,600) x 1e6 = $0.28 per 1M tokens
At 20% utilisation (spiky daytime traffic): $1.39 per 1M tokens
```

Then compare with the API's per-token price for a model of similar quality on your eval. Hidden costs on the self-hosted side:

| Factor | API | Self-hosted |
|---|---|---|
| Idle capacity | You pay per token | You pay per GPU-hour, busy or not |
| Engineering and on-call | Provider's problem | Yours: upgrades, autoscaling, outages |
| Model quality ceiling | Frontier closed models available | Open-weight models only |
| Data control and residency | Contract and region options | Full control |
| Latency control | Shared, rate-limited | Tunable; can co-locate |
| Customisation | Limited fine-tuning | Any fine-tune, LoRA, decoding constraint |

Rule of thumb: start on APIs; consider self-hosting when you have steady high volume, a task an open model handles well (proven by evals), strict data requirements, or a need for custom models. Many teams end up hybrid: a small self-hosted or cheap hosted model for high-volume simple tasks, a frontier API for hard ones, with a router in between.

## Choosing a serving stack

| Need | Common choice |
|---|---|
| High-throughput GPU serving, OpenAI-compatible API | vLLM, SGLang |
| Maximum NVIDIA performance with compilation | TensorRT-LLM |
| Local / CPU / laptop | llama.cpp (GGUF), Ollama |
| Managed open-model hosting | Inference providers and cloud model gardens |

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

Serving questions separate people who have used an API from people who can run and cost an LLM feature. Expect one memory calculation (KV cache or weights), one explanation of why decode is slow, and one trade-off discussion (latency vs throughput, API vs self-hosted, quantisation vs quality).

## Questions with model answers

### 1. Why is the first token slow and the rest fast (or the reverse)?

**Model answer.** The first token requires prefill: a forward pass over the entire prompt, which is compute-bound and grows with prompt length (attention quadratically), plus any queueing. After that, each token is one decode step that reads the weights and KV cache once; it is memory-bandwidth-bound and roughly constant per token, growing slowly with context. So long prompts hurt TTFT, long outputs hurt total latency. Prefix caching cuts TTFT for repeated prefixes; quantisation and speculative decoding cut TPOT.

### 2. How much KV cache does a 32-layer model with 8 KV heads of size 128 need for 32 users at 4k context in FP16?

**Model answer.** Per token: `2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB`. Per user at 4,096 tokens: 512 MiB. For 32 users: 16 GiB. With 16 GB of BF16 weights for an 8B model, that fits on one 40 GB or 80 GB GPU with room for activations. With full multi-head attention (32 KV heads) it would be 64 GiB, which would not fit beside the weights on a 40 GB card.

### 3. Explain continuous batching and PagedAttention. How do they relate?

**Model answer.** Continuous batching schedules at the granularity of a single decode step: finished sequences leave and waiting ones join every iteration, so the GPU is not held hostage by the longest request. PagedAttention manages KV memory in fixed-size blocks with a per-sequence block table, allocated on demand, so memory is not reserved for the maximum length and fragmentation is nearly eliminated. They are complementary: paging frees memory, continuous batching fills that memory with more concurrent sequences, and together they raise throughput by several times over static batching.

### 4. What does quantising to 4-bit buy you and what does it cost?

**Model answer.** Weights shrink about 4x versus BF16, so a model fits on smaller or fewer GPUs and memory-bound decode gets faster because fewer bytes are read per token. Costs: some quality loss that is uneven across skills, dequantisation overhead that reduces gains for compute-bound prefill and large batches, and kernel support varies by hardware. I would compare BF16, FP8 and INT4 versions on our eval set and latency benchmark before choosing, and consider FP8 KV cache separately since it affects concurrency.

### 5. How does speculative decoding speed things up without changing outputs?

**Model answer.** A cheap drafter proposes k tokens; the target model verifies all of them in a single forward pass, which costs about the same as generating one token because decode is memory-bound. Tokens are accepted with a rejection-sampling rule that provably preserves the target's distribution, and one extra token comes from the target. Speedup depends on acceptance rate, so it is best on predictable outputs and at low to moderate batch sizes.

### 6. Users complain the chatbot "feels slow". How do you investigate?

**Model answer.** Break latency into parts with tracing: network and auth, retrieval and tool calls, queueing, TTFT, TPOT, output length. Look at p95, not averages. Typical fixes by cause: stream tokens to the UI if we are not; shrink or cache the prompt prefix to cut TTFT; run retrieval in parallel with other steps; reduce output length with instructions or max tokens; route simple requests to a smaller model; for reasoning models, lower the reasoning effort where quality allows. Then set an SLO (for example TTFT p95 under 1 second) and track it.

### 7. When would you self-host an open model instead of using an API?

**Model answer.** When volume is high and steady enough to keep GPUs busy, an open model passes our evals for the task, data control or residency requires it, or we need customisation the API does not offer (custom fine-tunes, constrained decoding, specific latency). I would compute cost per million tokens from measured throughput and realistic utilisation, add engineering and on-call cost, and compare with API pricing. For spiky or low traffic, or tasks needing frontier quality, the API usually wins.

### 8. What is the difference between TTFT, TPOT and throughput, and which would you optimise for a chat UI vs a batch job?

**Model answer.** TTFT is the wait until the first token, TPOT the gap between tokens, throughput the total tokens per second across requests. A chat UI is latency-sensitive: optimise TTFT p95 and keep TPOT below reading speed, accepting smaller batches. An overnight batch job (classification, summarisation of a backlog) should maximise throughput and cost efficiency with large batches, or use a provider's batch API, which typically trades latency for a lower price.

## Common mistakes

- Sizing GPUs from weights alone and forgetting the KV cache.
- Assuming temperature 0 means bit-for-bit reproducible output.
- Reporting average latency instead of percentiles.
- Comparing self-hosted cost at 100% utilisation with API prices.
- Quantising and shipping based on a perplexity number, not task evals.

## Numbers to remember

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| KV bytes per token | 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes |
| BF16 weights | 2 bytes per parameter |
| Decode lower bound at batch 1 | weight bytes / memory bandwidth |
| vLLM default block size | 16 tokens |
| End-to-end latency | TTFT + TPOT x (n - 1) |

keyPoints: Prefill is compute-bound and sets TTFT; decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and sets TPOT.
KV cache bytes per token = 2 x layers x KV heads x head dim x bytes; at long context it, not weights, limits concurrency.
Sampling (temperature, top-p, min-p, penalties, constrained decoding) shapes output; temperature 0 is not fully deterministic.
Continuous batching plus PagedAttention keep GPUs full and KV waste low, giving several-fold throughput gains.
Quantisation and speculative decoding mainly speed up decode; verify quality on your own evals.
Compare self-hosting and APIs with cost per million tokens at realistic utilisation, plus engineering cost.

check.q: Why does weight-only 4-bit quantisation speed up single-user decoding almost proportionally?
options: It reduces the number of layers
Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, so fewer bytes per weight means faster token steps
It removes the need for a KV cache
It makes attention linear in sequence length
check.why: At small batch sizes each decode step reads every weight once; cutting bytes per weight cuts the time spent waiting on memory.

check.q: A model has 40 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, FP16 KV. Roughly how much KV cache does one 10,000-token sequence need?
options: About 160 KB
About 16 MB
About 16 GB
About 1.6 GB
check.why: 2 x 40 x 8 x 128 x 2 bytes = 163,840 bytes per token; times 10,000 tokens is about 1.6 GB.

check.q: What does continuous batching change compared with static batching?
options: Sequences join and leave the batch at every decode step instead of waiting for the whole batch to finish
It batches requests by prompt length only
It runs prefill and decode on the CPU
It removes the need for KV memory management
check.why: Iteration-level scheduling frees finished slots immediately and admits new requests, raising utilisation for variable-length outputs.
